newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - Markets seen calm about Polish cabinet shake-up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Markets seen calm about Polish cabinet shake-up.

text.p: Poland's liberal privatisation minister lost his job on Tuesday as the first casualty of a major government reform but became deputy chief of a new treasury ministry in a move likely to reassure markets.
Wieslaw Kaczmarek, seen as a champion of reforms in three leftist coalition cabinets since 1993, was replaced as his portfolio was taken over by a new, powerful treasury ministry.

In a compromise with the smaller Polish Peasant Party (PSL) -- often critical of privatisation deals -- Kaczmarek's ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) conceded the new ministry to PSL's Miroslaw Pietrewicz, hitherto head of the planning ministry.

Kaczmarek at first sidestepped appeals from his party's chiefs to stay on as deputy minister and as a guarantor that reforms would stay on track, but was later sworn in alongside Pietrewicz by President Aleksander Kwasniewski.

His appointment was likely to do much to dispel any concerns over the Peasant party's frequent reluctance to move boldly with privatisation, which made some market commentators uneasy over Pietrewicz's future course.
But even before Kaczmarek's surprise appointment, analysts said the leftist coalition's economic policy was likely to stay consistent.

"I think this reshuffle won't have a major impact on the economy and the markets...I see it more in terms of infighting within the coalition than any policy change," said Tomasz Jedrzejczak, securities analyst at Bank Handlowy SA brokerage.
"We may see some slow-down but no revolution," he said.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz -- who on Monday rushed to issue assurances that the government reform, far from slowing privatisation, would help it gain momentum -- had asked the reluctant Kaczmarek to accept the junior but crucial post.
Some analysts said they found Pietrewicz's views on the state's role in the economy disturbing but it was not clear how far the Peasants would get their way in the reformed cabinet.

"Mr. Pietrewicz seems to support an idea of greater state intervention in the economy and as treasury minister he may not be willing to see state assets depleted," one independent economist, who asked not to be named, said.

But he said it seemed unlikely the more reform-minded SLD would surrender control over economic policy to the Peasants and it might use the clout of the new powerful economy portfolio to achieve a counterbalance to the treasury minister's appointment.
Under the deal with the Peasants the SLD will take over the economy ministry when it is created on January 1.
Analysts said foreign investors were awaiting a clear statement from Pietrewicz of his views on privatisation.
"The markets wait for a clear signal whether and how his policy will differ from Kaczmarek's," said Jacek Dzierwa, Polish equity analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
But Poland's determination to join the European Union and NATO should prevent any radical departures from structural reforms and fiscal discipline, he added.

Analysts also said the fact that Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko was likely to stay on as a guardian of fiscal discipline, despite earlier speculation that he also might lose his job in the shake-up, was a further positive signal.
"The important point is that Kolodko will remain in charge of the economy," said Tim Drinkall, chief analyst at Creditanstalt Securities in Warsaw.
